newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan panel told no holds barred in nuclear review.
newsitem.headline: Japan panel told no holds barred in nuclear review.

text.p: The Japanese government told a panel of crisis experts on Friday to leave no holds barred in proposing reforms in the state-run firm accused of misreporting and covering up a succession of nuclear accidents.

"We ask you to conduct a fundamental review of the corporation, and this includes the possibility of a complete disbandment," Science and Technology Minister Riichiro Chikaoka told the first meeting of the nine-member panel.
The series of misreported accidents and cover-ups by the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC) has shocked Japan, a country always nervous about nuclear power.
The panel, chaired by former Tokyo University Dean Hiroyuki Yoshioka, is to draft its final report by the end of July.
Earlier this week, the government took the rare step of filing a criminal complaint against the PNC for falsifying formal reports about Japan's worst nuclear accident.

The March 11 explosion at a nuclear fuel reprocessing plant at Tokaimura, north of Tokyo, exposed 37 staff to low levels of radiation. Last week, PNC officials admitted a cover-up of the way plant managers handled the accident and police have begun investigating the case.
Just after the Tokaimura cover-up was revealed, PNC admitted that it failed to report a dozen radiation leaks at its advanced thermal reactor "Fugen" over the past three years.

Fugen, located at Tsuruga on the coast of the Sea of Japan some 350 km (220 miles) west of Tokyo, is Japan's only reactor to use heavy water. In the latest leak accident at Fugen on Monday night, 11 staff were exposed to low levels of radiation.
Fugen was ordered shut down on Tuesday night.

The Tokaimura reprocessing plant, Japan's only such facility, which handled 12 percent of the country's spent nuclear fuel, is also closed. The rest of Japan's spent nuclear fuel is reprocessed at French plants.
These scandals followed a damaging December 1995 affair over a massive coolant leak at Monju, a fast-breeder reactor also located at Tsuruga.
After officials admitted PNC suppressed details and video tape of the leakage, a PNC official in charge of the probe committed suicide. Monju has remained shutdown since then.

PNC is at the heart of Japan's ambitions to use more recycled nuclear fuel and boost electricity output from nuclear plants to 42 percent of total power needs by 2010. Nuclear plants now supply a third of Japan's total power output.

But the latest accidents meant that only two of its six primary facilities are still running. In addition to Fugen, Monju and the Tokaimura plant, a nuclear fuel production plant near Tokaimura has been closed since March, when a false criticality alarm went off.
The expert panel was formed on the orders of Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who demanded that a third-party body, and not Chikaoka's Science and Technology Agency, conduct a review of the PNC.
Chikaoka, the cabinet member whose agency oversees the PNC, is now under fire from an angry opposition.

The main opposition group Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) submitted a no-confidence motion to parliament against Chikaoka on Friday although Hashimoto's ruling party and its allies look set to kill the motion off in a plenary session next week.
